title: Data Types
summary: Pick the right MySQL column type: integer sizes and UNSIGNED, DECIMAL versus FLOAT, CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT, DATE, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP, ENUM, BOOLEAN and JSON, and what strict mode does with.
introduction: Every column has a type, and the type decides three things: which values are accepted, how much disk and memory each row uses, and how comparisons behave. Choosing FLOAT for prices or TIMESTAMP for birthdays causes bugs that surface months later. This lesson walks through the families of MySQL types with small experiments you can run in the client, explains what strict mode does when a value does not fit, and ends with the JSON type for data that refuses to sit in columns.
learningObjectives: Choose integer and decimal types that fit the range and precision you need
Tell CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT apart and size them in characters, not bytes
Explain how DATETIME and TIMESTAMP differ and when to use each
Use ENUM, BOOLEAN and JSON columns appropriately

blocks.text: Integer types differ only in size, and size decides the range. Adding `UNSIGNED` forbids negatives and doubles the positive range (`INT UNSIGNED` reaches 4,294,967,295), which suits quantities and ids. The old display width, as in `INT(11)`, has been deprecated since 8.0.17 and is no longer shown by `SHOW CREATE TABLE`; it never limited the stored value anyway.

rows: ids on huge tables, money in cents
exact, `p` digits of which `s` after the point
prices, rates, anything you add up

blocks.text: Arithmetic has MySQL-specific rules worth seeing once. `/` always produces a decimal result with four extra decimal places, `DIV` is integer division and `MOD` (or `%`) is the remainder.

A literal with a decimal point, such as `0.1`, is a `DECIMAL` and is exact. Writing it as `0.1E0` makes it a `DOUBLE`, a binary floating-point number that cannot represent one tenth exactly. The comparison below is why prices belong in `DECIMAL`: with floats, three items at 0.1 do not add up to 0.3.

What happens when a value does not fit is decided by `sql_mode`. The default since 5.7 includes `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES`, so an out-of-range number, an overlong string or an unknown `ENUM` value is an error and the statement is rolled back. The second insert fits and succeeds.

blocks.content:
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.02 sec)

ERROR 1264 (22003): Out of range value for column 'qty' at row 1
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.01 sec)

blocks.title: Do not switch strict mode off
blocks.text: Old tutorials suggest removing `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES` so that a failing insert goes through. It then succeeds by silently storing 255 instead of 300, an empty string for an invalid ENUM value and a truncated string for an overlong VARCHAR, with only a warning that nobody reads. Fix the data or widen the column instead; the default modes exist to protect you.

rows: fixed-length codes such as a country `CHAR(2)`
65,535 bytes per row, shared by all columns
length prefix plus the bytes used
small fixed vocabularies such as a status
hashes and small files; keep large files in object storage

blocks.text: Lengths are declared in *characters*, and with `utf8mb4` a character can take four bytes, so `VARCHAR(255)` may occupy 1,020 bytes. `CHAR_LENGTH()` counts characters and `LENGTH()` counts bytes; the accented letter below is one character and two bytes.

blocks.code: SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('café') AS chars, LENGTH('café') AS bytes;

blocks.text: An `ENUM` is stored as a small integer index into its list, so it is compact and fast, but it has two surprises: it sorts by position in the definition rather than alphabetically, and adding a value means an `ALTER TABLE`. Inserting a value that is not in the list fails under strict mode with `ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'roast' at row 1`. Use it for lists that genuinely never grow; for anything else, a lookup table with a foreign key is easier to extend.

rows: stored exactly as written; no time zone
converted to UTC on write and to the session time zone on read
a time of day or a duration

blocks.text: The difference between `DATETIME` and `TIMESTAMP` only shows when the session time zone changes, which is exactly what happens when an application server in one region talks to a database in another. Store the same value in both, then read it back from a different zone:

The `DATETIME` came back unchanged; the `TIMESTAMP` was stored as UTC and shifted to the new session zone. Use `TIMESTAMP` (or `DATETIME` with every session set to UTC) for *when something happened*, and `DATE` or `DATETIME` for wall-clock facts such as a birthday or an appointment that must not move. The optional `fsp` is the number of fractional-second digits, up to 6; `DATETIME(3)` keeps milliseconds. Audit columns usually read `created_at DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`.

`BOOLEAN` is a synonym for `TINYINT(1)`: `TRUE` is stored as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, and `WHERE active` works because any non-zero number is true. A `JSON` column stores a validated document in a binary format that can be indexed through generated columns. `JSON_OBJECT` and `JSON_ARRAY` build documents, and MySQL prints them with its own normalised spacing:

`JSON_EXTRACT` reads a path and returns JSON, quotes included; `JSON_UNQUOTE` turns it into a plain string. On a JSON *column* the operators `->` and `->>` are shorthand for the same two calls, as in `payload->>'$.name'`.

blocks.code:
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT('{"name": "Priya"}', '$.name') AS extracted,
       JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT('{"name": "Priya"}', '$.name')) AS unquoted;

blocks.text: MySQL 9.0 added a `VECTOR(n)` type for machine-learning embeddings, created from text with `STRING_TO_VECTOR('[0.1, 0.2, ...]')`. It is not available in 8.4, which is one example of why a lesson may say *9.x only*.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Pick the smallest type that fits every value you will ever store, add `NOT NULL` unless absence is meaningful, use `DECIMAL` for money, and put anything you need to filter on into a real column rather than inside JSON.

questions.question: Which type should hold a customer's date of birth?
questions.explanation: A birthday is a calendar fact with no time zone. DATE stores exactly the day written; TIMESTAMP would convert it between zones and cannot represent dates before 1970.

questions.question: With the default sql_mode, inserting 300 into a `TINYINT UNSIGNED` column stores 255 and continues.
questions.explanation: STRICT_TRANS_TABLES is on by default, so an out-of-range value is an error (1264) and nothing is stored. Only with strict mode disabled would MySQL clip the value to 255.
